PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis.
